title: New Skills and AI Are Reshaping the Future of Work
date_evidence: Author byline 'Kristalina Georgieva' followed by dateline 'January 14, 2026'
key_claim: One in 10 job postings in advanced economies now require at least one new skill; job postings with a new skill pay about 3 percent more, rising to 8.5 to 15 percent for four or more new skills; employment in AI-vulnerable occupations is 3.6 percent lower after five years in high-AI-skill-demand regions; Finland, Ireland and Denmark top the IMF Skill Readiness Index.
signals_supported: Reskilling imperative and shortening skill half-life

title: The OECD AI exposure measure
date_evidence: OECD AI exposure measure publication page; finds occupations at highest risk of automation account for about 28 percent of jobs across OECD countries, with most exposed workers needing changed tasks rather than specialised AI skills.
key_claim: The OECD AI exposure measure finds AI capabilities are closest to routine information-processing and administrative work; occupations at highest risk of automation account for about 28 percent of jobs across OECD countries, and most exposed workers will see tasks change rather than need specialised AI skills.
signals_supported: Reskilling imperative and shortening skill half-life

title: Reskilling Revolution: Preparing 1 billion people for tomorrow's economy
date_evidence: Visible dateline 'Published Jan 23, 2026 · Updated Mar 9, 2026' on the article page
key_claim: By 2030, 22 percent of jobs are expected to be disrupted (170 million new roles, 92 million displaced); 39 percent of workers' core skills are anticipated to change by 2030 as AI moves into workflows; only 0.5 percent of global GDP is invested in adult lifelong learning, and the longevity of technical skills is shortening.
signals_supported: Reskilling imperative and shortening skill half-life

title: State of the Global Workplace 2026
date_evidence: Search result: 'Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2026 report was released on April 8, 2026... global employee engagement fell to 20% in 2025, its lowest level since 2020'.
key_claim: Global employee engagement fell to 20 percent in 2025, its lowest level since 2020 and the first two consecutive years of decline, costing an estimated $10 trillion in lost productivity; manager engagement fell from 27 percent to 22 percent between 2024 and 2025, and the direct manager is the strongest predictor of whether an employee adopts AI.

title: Inside the AI Index: 12 Takeaways from the 2026 Report
date_evidence: Author 'Shana Lynch' with dateline 'April 13, 2026' on the article page
key_claim: AI's workforce disruption has moved from prediction to reality, hitting young workers first: employment among software developers aged 22 to 25 fell nearly 20 percent since 2024 even as older cohorts grew, with the same pattern in other high-exposure jobs such as customer service.

title: The 'forever layoffs' era hits a recession trigger as corporates sack 1.1 million workers through November
date_evidence: Visible dateline 'December 9, 2025, 10:00 AM ET' (authors Nick Lichtenberg and Eva Roytburg)
key_claim: US-based employers announced 1,170,821 job cuts in the first 11 months of 2025, up 54 percent year on year and only the sixth year since 1993 to top 1.1 million through November; 'forever layoffs' (rolling cuts of fewer than 50 workers) now make up a majority of cuts, AI has been blamed for more than 70,000 announced cuts since 2023, and announced hiring is at its lowest year-to-date level since 2010.

title: Surviving the Great Flattening: The coming extinction of the middle manager
date_evidence: Visible dateline 'September 19, 2025, 8:00 AM ET' (author George Pesansky)
key_claim: Gartner found that through 2026, 20 percent of organizations surveyed will use AI to flatten their organizational structure, eliminating over half of their current middle-management positions, as AI puts knowledge at everyone's fingertips and shifts the premium from knowing answers to executing with consistency.

title: 5 days in the office is the least popular way to work. Bosses are mandating it anyway
date_evidence: Search result: 'according to a CNBC article from February 2, 2026' covering why bosses mandate five-day office schedules; more than half of Fortune 100 companies moved from hybrid to fully in-office, with Stellantis and Home Depot the latest to require five days.
key_claim: Five days in the office is the least popular work setup, especially for workers in their 20s and 30s, yet more than half of Fortune 100 companies have moved from hybrid to fully in-office policies, with Stellantis and Home Depot the latest major employers to require five days a week alongside Amazon, Instagram and Paramount.

title: The automation illusion: Why AI is making COOs' jobs harder, not easier
date_evidence: meta og:url /2026/06/01/ and visible dateline 'June 1, 2026, 7:37 PM ET' (author Nick Lichtenberg)

signals_supported: AI agents enter the org as coworkers

title: Cognizant CEO is swimming against the tide on AI: he's hiring over 20,000 graduates this year and says AI tokenmaxxing is a 'vanity metric'
date_evidence: meta og:url /2026/06/01/ and visible dateline 'June 1, 2026, 7:40 PM ET' (author Preston Fore)
key_claim: Cognizant CEO Ravi Kumar S. said the firm hired 20,000 entry-level graduates last year and expects more in 2026, calling an entry-level jobs collapse 'fearmongering'; he predicts the workforce pyramid will flatten with leaner middle layers, and notes OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have walked back earlier AI-jobs-apocalypse predictions.

title: Skill-based hiring in 2026: the 85% vs 0.14% paradox
key_claim: 85 percent of employers told TestGorilla they use skills-based hiring, while Harvard Business School and the Burning Glass Institute found fewer than 1 in 700 new hires (0.14 percent) were workers without a bachelor's degree; 53 percent of employers had publicly removed degree requirements, up from 30 percent the prior year, but the practice trails the policy.

title: The end of the middle: What happens when the layer disappears
date_evidence: Visible 'Date May 20, 2026' with author 'Alexei Dunaway' on the article page
key_claim: Bayer cut management layers from 11-12 to 6-7 with average span of control now 14 (some managers carrying 90 reports) and about 5,500 roles eliminated; Amazon cut roughly 14,000 corporate roles in October 2025 and lifted its individual-contributor-to-manager ratio; Meta is cutting 8,000 more roles with spans reportedly reaching 50 to 1; Korn Ferry found 41 percent of employees saw layers trimmed and 37 percent who lost a manager felt directionless.
